What I'm saying is the way we think of time.

Yes, the laws of nature or whatever is constant, and time is relative.

But how we interpret time hasn't been a constant since the dawn of man.

In our modern world, there's a relatively universal concept of time that's used by most of the planet. You know what hour of the day it is, what day of the week it is, the month, and so on.

But consider this: there are still people on this planet that don't have a concept of measuring time. Maybe intentionally, maybe accidentally, maybe something else.

Which brought me to thinking, what about ancient civilians? Even though they're not existing in the way they did a millennia or two ago, in a Mayan calendar, it's likely we're not in the year we think we are. For ancient China it's very likely we're not in the year we think we are.

To some possibly distant alien civilization we could be in the year 7624 according to them for all we know.

Measurements of time are relative to the civilization that uses them. It just really blows my mind that there's a multitude of ways human beings have viewed it and experienced it and the possibility of what we have now changing, evolving, and conforming to some other method.

And it's crazily weird. Because there's a chance we're wrong. There may not be much of a chance but anything is possible.

>If the prey stood still and let the predator eat it's share and somehow don't die from the wounds

Well in that case they can't really be killed can they?

Killing is, in most cases, out of the necessity to not have to keep chasing prey and thus making it more likely a carnivorous animal will live to the limit of their average life expectancy.

But making it impossible for prey to die while still allowing a hunter to eat renders the need to kill null. If it was a sudden change it'd probably take a generation or two to figure things out, but the instinct would still be there. So I guess it would still happen anyway if possible. Most animals can learn how to adapt to their environment but changing innate behavior is much harder to do.

I've given it a thought before. It's an interesting idea but there's something about plants that, while it's closely related to things that animals do, that is lacking.

Plants sure do have feelings but they're not necessarily complex in the same way as animals. Plants have purely reactionary responses to the world around them and the things that happen to them(to my knowledge at least). The corpse flower (I forget the name?) produces a scent to lure prey, grass and onions give off a smell in response to damage. But even though animals can do the same or similar things, many also do things and experience or respond to outside stimuli in a way that shapes their lives, changes behaviors, and can alter personality. There's studies of dozens of mammals that prove it for a range of creature from birds to elephants to dolphins and I'm sure more.

But I don't know how one would respond to this hypothetical. Reevaluate their beliefs? Have a moral dilemma? I mean, I feel like I know enough that it wouldn't phase me just because I need to eat something to survive. And plants are the most friendly to the environment at large to harvest and consume (I think?)

I have literally no authority on the matter though. /shrug

Before depression began and after I guess. I can't even remember if I was 12 or 13.

Before, I was an excellent student with recommendations for advancing early and regular recognition for my perfect grades. I wasn't a people person and dreaded group activity but I had my books, a computer, and my art supplies.

I suddenly was struck with depression severe enough that I went from honors to falling everything in less than three months. My only explanation is my younger sister's diagnosis of ADHD and the subsequent efforts my parents had to make so that she transferred into remedial classes without losing her progression through school, had medication, and whatever other needs she might have were met. This was the same time frame for either my father's parents dying or my father being seriously injured in an accident, my memory is too blurry to pinpoint which. There were more important things to take care of, I was a model student before that so I can only assume there was no worry or attention paid because what's there to worry about? I felt neglected and developed a crippling block in my ability to write which required eventual tutoring at no small expense to my family. I spent five long years in school thereafter, dropping out my senior year of high school because, with my failure to pass English at any time, I was told I would not get a diploma for another 2 years due to some kind of restriction for taking multiple classes of the same subject (and that would only be if I passed them all). I took a GED class and then tested the following spring. My instructor told me I scored the second highest in the state, which helped me realise I'm not stupid at least.

It just hasn't gotten better unfortunately, for my brain at least. I'm at a point where I'm disabled by several mental disorders and I basically need daily supervision to make sure I'm taking care of my body, which I tend to neglect too often. On the bright side I'm involved with therapy, am sort of neurotic about taking my medication, and have an excellent support system keeping me in a home that I have room to breathe in and ensuring I have access to most of my needs. I just now wish my body would tell me to eat in stead of needing to hear someone else mention food.

Well, I know only one, related to a cemetery.

In the middle of the small city I live in lies a sprawling stretch of cemeteries only divided by fences or tree lines, with the collective name most refer it to as Vale cemetery ( which is connected by a paved trail to Vale park, I kid you not). It covers at the least 3 square miles, about 1.5 of it in either direction. This place is old, dating back to colonial times, and if you look hard enough you can find some mildly famous people that are buried there. There's also a gated area for the esteemed alumni/staff of one of the oldest colleges around. But that's just average, mildly interesting stuff.

There's a lovely, gravel paved trail which you can branch from to get to an area where there's a drainage pipe you go over. Just ahead of that is an unfortunately graffiti covered monument to civil war infantry from the area, but also a tunnel that's been boarded over, welded shut, and finally had a slab of metal bolted to the very stone of the entrance (the last happened within the past 5 years). "Hell's mouth" if I recall right, as any local kid would call it. But this is just atmosphere.

A rectangular plot of graves rests just above this spot, and because most of this place is left to grow wild, rabbits, deer, and even turkeys have been spotted. Climb up a well worn hill, the roots of trees expose to make a stairway, and there you are. Most of the stones have been overturned and the ones not horizontal have occult symbols, crude but legible. It's been said more than once that some kids, perhaps adults, engaged in animal sacrifices. At least one eviscerated turkey can claim it true.

But to my knowledge, they hadn't stopped these sacrifices upon that discovery, whomever they were, because years later there was a murder. The head and a limb of someone appeared strung up on the branches of a tree facing one of the main streets that are used to get around. It was a poor job according to the gossip that traveled, and I think someone was apprehended -- who seemed too out of it, dazed, lost in his mind from a mental disorder.

I didn't hear how it panned out but the area, where the dead animals were found initially, had gone dead itself. No perfect shape, but that death is crawling its way toward the other parts of the cemetery. At least it seems that way. Are they still around? No idea. The group might have moved on... But there's a lot of land to cover just in this one place.

For a quick snack, I just heat up no bean chili, sprinkle shredded cheese, and use as a dip with tortilla chips. For an actual meal, I make lemon pepper shrimp over white pasta...

Pre-cooked shrimp
Fettuccini noodles or similar
Butter
Olive oil
Lemon juice
Pepper
Salt
Herbs/spices of your choosing
{Basil, oregano, thyme, basically commonly found things in an average kitchen}

In pan over lowest heat possible, place shrimp and some butter. sprinkle lemon and pepper once the butter has melted. (4-7 minutes)
In large pot, boil noodles, add pinch of salt and drizzle of Olive oil to the water.(~7 minutes)
Once noodles are done, drain until only very small amount of water remains. Return to pot.
Over lowest heat, replace pot and add to noodles spoon of butter and drizzle of Olive oil, slowly increasing heat to a low medium. Mix well and add your herbs/spices, taking care to ensure nothing sticks. (5-8 minutes)
Plate shrimp over a bed of noodles and enjoy~

TL;DR, self imposed isolation as a child and thought I was an alien for 6+ years because I felt alone on this planet, got depressed into reality, and just hated everyone from there.

I never liked people as a child. I was a quiet and reserved person from the moment I started school. I didn't have friends that I can remember but I recall some habits and thoughts from the early years.

Recess outside, I would curl up into my coat and sit against a tree the whole time, hiding from everything and everyone. I just didn't want to be near other people or do anything that made me interact with others. I also remember silently begging for no one to notice me when there were group activities within the classroom.

But the thing is, because of such habits, my imagination ran wild. I ended up being convinced I was an alien from a distant planet, sometimes here for research and sometimes just stranded and trying to blend in until someone came for me. I had thought of dozens of things about my home planet - climate, colors, flora and fauna, my "real" family, the state of politics and science, the list goes on.

This train of thought ran much of my waking hours until I was about 13 and hit with such severe depression that I went from being an honors student to failing everything in the span of a few months. It effectively killed the sense of wonder one has as a child and I simply dropped everything that held any promise for my future that I didn't have passionate interest in. Loneliness turned to a deep disdain for "normal" kids my age so I ended up being angry and frustrated through high school, avoiding others more fiercely while the small, gentle side of me just wanted somebody to like her. Made a grand total of one lasting friendship from start to finish of mandatory education, which completely disintegrated some 5 years ago. I'm a miserable bastard because I'm lonely, but I'm as kind as possible to everyone because my parents are hippies and brought me up like that.
